extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comedy/TV writers, podcast listeners interested in comedy craft and moral-philosophy-in-comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and performing comedy (especially TV/sitcom/SNL-style) and for making complex ideas (like moral philosophy) accessible and entertaining. Drawn from an interview with Michael Schur about his process, writers' rooms, and audience-facing comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not be precious with your own material
rubrics_metrics.description: “The thing that SNL teaches you is to not be precious with your own material.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to discard or rapidly revise jokes and bits; treat your writing as material to be tested rather than sacred. SNL's environment is cited as training writers to let go of attachment to their lines so the strongest material survives. Anti-pattern: defending a joke despite repeated negative audience/room reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use audience feedback as real-time testing (perform for the room)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Comedy for performance, it’s like the Roman Coliseum. A bunch of people give you a thumbs up or a thumbs down, and then it’s up to you to figure out what to do next.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat live/performance/audience reaction as immediate data; iterate quickly based on that signal. If a bit fails repeatedly, rework or drop it. The interview frames performing as an experimental process where audience responses guide creative decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succeed through rapid, collaborative iteration (SNL-style training)
rubrics_metrics.description: SNL trains writers in a rapid, collaborative environment where material is constantly judged and revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value speed, collaboration, and the ability to take and implement critique from peers. Working in high-tempo writers’ rooms teaches resilience and judgement about what’s working. Example: Schur suggests Hollywood creatives would benefit from SNL-style experience. Anti-pattern: isolationist writing that never sees test audiences or peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make complex ideas conversational and non-condescending
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you could somehow take what they wrote, synthesize it, and talk about it conversationally with people in a way that isn’t condescending, but it is engaging, then that might be of use to people.” (about adapting dense philosophy for a general audience)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When integrating big ideas (e.g., moral philosophy) into comedy, synthesize and translate dense material into approachable, conversational language. Aim to be engaging without talking down to the audience. Example guidance comes from Schur’s aim for his book to do for philosophy what a popular science book does for astrophysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame heavy topics (ethics) as practical life-improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: “I just recommend ethics as a life improvement strategy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comedy engages with ethical or philosophical themes, present them as practically useful to the audience — actionable or illustrative — rather than abstract lecturing. This framing makes serious subject matter more resonant and usable for viewers/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn via apprenticeship and strong showrunner mentorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Schur describes working with The Office showrunner Greg Daniels as a pivotal learning experience: a kind of “TV university.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize hands-on learning in established writers’ rooms and seek mentorship from experienced showrunners; structural craft, pacing, and character work are often learned through apprenticeship. Example: Schur cites his time on The Office as teaching things SNL did not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply structural/force-based principles to character development (the 'F = ma' of sitcom writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to the “F = ma of sitcom writing” as guiding character development on The Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters so that clear motivating 'forces' (beliefs, needs, pressures) produce believable, consistent actions — analogous to applying a causal principle to behavior. Use those forces to generate conflict, jokes, and character-driven plot. Scoring note: characters that behave consistently according to their internal logic are stronger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed fiction/comedy from specific, everyday incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: The seed of The Good Place idea came from an outrageous car repair bill; everyday occurrences can spark show concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for vivid, concrete real-life moments or absurdities as inspiration for premises, scenes, or jokes. Specificity often yields more original and resonant comedic material than abstract brainstorming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult domain experts when comedy intersects with specialized subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Todd May and Pamela Hieronymi were used as emergency contacts for The Good Place writers’ room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a comedy relies on philosophical/technical accuracy (e.g., ethics in The Good Place), consult actual scholars/experts to avoid misrepresentation and to enrich the material. This increases credibility and can produce richer, more interesting jokes rooted in real ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine personal failures and anxieties for authentic material and growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Schur discusses his “most worthwhile failures (and one recurring failure that still gives him nightmares).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal setbacks as sources of honest material and learning rather than hiding them; failures can generate empathy, humility, and comedic insight. Anti-pattern: hiding vulnerability or sanitizing experiences so they lose emotional truth.
